content: 1. The extraction of teeth is performed when necessary to address dental issues such as severe decay, infection, or trauma. 2. Incision and drainage are carried out to manage dento-alveolar abscesses, which involve the removal of pus and infection from the affected area. 3. Medications are prescribed to treat infections of the orofacial and dento-alveolar regions, ensuring proper management of bacterial or other microbial causes. 4. A dental splint is used to stabilize mobile teeth caused by trauma, providing support and promoting healing. 5. Oral cancer and potentially malignant oral disorders are managed with timely referrals to appropriate specialists for diagnosis and treatment. 6. Oral manifestations of HIV and AIDS are addressed through targeted management strategies to alleviate symptoms and prevent complications. 7. Cleft lip and palate, as well as other orofacial developmental anomalies, are managed through multidisciplinary approaches to improve function and aesthetics. 8. An oral health unit within a ministry of health should ideally be fully integrated or aligned with units responsible for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), family health, life-course health, or other related areas. 9. Such a unit is typically guided by a national oral health policy or similar framework, led by dedicated staff with expertise in public health and administration, and included in the ministry’s overall budgeting process. 10. The operational and logistical functions of an oral health unit within the broader healthcare system are fundamental and should be adapted to align with national priorities and principles. 11. National governments play a critical role in strengthening advocacy and political commitment for oral health, adapting regional action plans to national contexts, and prioritizing feasible actions to improve oral health outcomes. 12. Governments are responsible for developing policies, legislation, standards, and regulations to integrate oral health with NCDs, primary healthcare (PHC), and universal health coverage (UHC). 13. Adequate budgetary and resource allocation for oral health is essential, along with coordination across ministries to ensure oral health promotion and disease prevention are part of broader agendas. 14. Subnational administrations should include and prioritize oral health in planning and implementation frameworks, provide capacity building, and engage communities to improve oral and general health. 15. Health regulatory bodies must establish legislation and regulations to enable effective implementation of national oral health plans, ensure proper licensing of professionals, and promote quality facilities. 16. Professional associations should design and conduct activities for continuous professional development, maintain ethical standards, and advocate for oral health at all decision-making levels. 17. Educational and research institutions should support training curricula that meet national needs and international standards, recommend evidence-based approaches for oral disease management, and conduct research to inform policy. 18. Media organizations should support advocacy efforts and raise awareness about oral health-related issues. 19. Development and implementation partners should integrate oral health into interventions addressing common NCD risk factors, provide technical support, and promote sustainable investment in oral health programs. 20. Communities, families, and individuals should actively participate in local oral health initiatives, advocate for community-based programs, and support the implementation of policies such as smoke-free environments and improved hygiene practices. 21. Individuals and communities should engage in activities that improve access to oral healthcare for all age groups and act as role models to promote oral health awareness and behavior change.
